summary: New Generation Software published early British 3D and arcade-style games across the ZX81, ZX Spectrum and Commodore 64, with Malcolm E. Evans closely associated with several of its best-documented releases.
facts: The Centre for Computing History preserves ten New Generation Software releases, beginning with early ZX81 titles and extending into Commodore 64 software.
The museum catalogue records Malcolm E. Evans on titles including Escape, 3D Tunnel and Knot in 3D, while its Commodore 64 records include Shoot the Rapids.
note: The surviving institutional record is stronger for the software catalogue than for the company's corporate structure, so this profile remains catalogue-focused.

sources.label: Centre for Computing History — New Generation Software games

summary: Odin Computer Graphics was a Liverpool software house that emerged from the earlier Thor name and produced polished mid-1980s 8-bit games before its work became associated with Telecomsoft and Firebird.
facts: The Centre for Computing History records Odin as Liverpool-based and says the company had previously published games under the Thor name before adopting Odin Computer Graphics for in-house game development.
The museum identifies Nodes of Yesod as Odin's first release and records later Odin work appearing under Firebird after Telecomsoft became involved.
note: Odin's publishing and development roles changed as Telecomsoft and Firebird became involved, so individual CCG game credits remain authoritative for each release.

sources.label: Centre for Computing History — Odin Computer Graphics company profile

summary: Origin Systems was formed in 1983 by Richard Garriott and his brother Robert. The company became closely associated with computer role-playing games and the Ultima series before joining Electronic Arts in 1992.
facts: Richard Garriott's own history states that he teamed with his older brother Robert in 1983 to form Origin Systems Inc.
Ultima III: Exodus was the first game published under the Origin banner.
Garriott records that Origin joined Electronic Arts in 1992.
note: This profile uses Richard Garriott's first-person company history; CCG's individual release credits remain version-specific.

summary: Orpheus appears in the CCG Commodore 64 archive on a small group of mid-1980s releases, including Elidon. Reliable surviving company-level documentation is limited, so the archive avoids adding unsupported founder or ownership claims.
note: This is intentionally a conservative archive summary until stronger first-party or institutional company-history material can be located.

summary: Palace Software published distinctive British home-computer games during the mid-to-late 1980s, with its catalogue spanning action adventures, licensed work and the Barbarian series across the Commodore 64 and other platforms.
facts: The Centre for Computing History preserves fifteen Palace Software game records across multiple home-computer platforms.
Its Commodore records include Barbarian: The Ultimate Warrior, Barbarian II, Rim Runner and Stifflip & Co.
note: The museum catalogue documents Palace's publishing output; individual development teams remain credited separately on CCG game pages.

sources.label: Centre for Computing History — Palace Software games

summary: Parker Brothers brought arcade, licensed and original games to early home consoles and computers. Its preserved software catalogue includes Q*bert, Super Cobra, Star Wars titles and computer versions of Panama Joe.
facts: The Centre for Computing History preserves thirteen game records under the Parker Brothers publishing credit.
The museum catalogue includes early Atari releases alongside computer software, documenting Parker Brothers as a multi-platform video-game publisher during the early 1980s.
note: This profile concentrates on Parker Brothers' video-game publishing activity represented in the museum and CCG archives.

sources.label: Centre for Computing History — Parker Brothers games

summary: Piranha published a compact but memorable run of British 8-bit games during the second half of the 1980s, including licensed character titles and games developed by external teams.
facts: The Centre for Computing History preserves Commodore 64 Piranha releases including Rogue Trooper, Strike Force Cobra, Yogi Bear and Through the Trapdoor.
The museum records development work for Piranha releases by teams including Design Design, Five Ways Software and Don Priestley.
note: Piranha frequently worked with external developers, so CCG keeps development and publishing credits separate.

sources.label: Centre for Computing History — Piranha C64 games

summary: Players Software published budget-oriented 8-bit games during the latter half of the 1980s, with releases spread across the Commodore 64, ZX Spectrum and Amstrad CPC.
facts: The Centre for Computing History preserves eight Players Software game records across several 8-bit systems.
Its Commodore records include Auriga and Electrix, while the wider catalogue includes Joe Blade, Eagles Nest, Radius and Street Gang.
note: Surviving institutional documentation is catalogue-led, so this profile avoids unsupported ownership or founder claims.

sources.label: Centre for Computing History — Players Software games

summary: Quicksilva was an important early British home-computer publisher whose catalogue ranged from ZX81 and Spectrum software to Commodore 64 releases and later conversions.
facts: The Centre for Computing History preserves forty game records under the Quicksilva publishing credit.
The museum collection includes early titles from 1982 and Commodore 64 releases such as Aquaplane, Booga-Boo, Purple Turtles and Rupert and the Toymaker's Party.
note: The profile reflects documented publishing activity rather than attempting to reconstruct unsupported corporate details.

sources.label: Centre for Computing History — Quicksilva games

summary: Rainbow Arts published games across 8-bit and 16-bit home computers, with a strong European catalogue that included Turrican, X-Out, Rock 'n Roll and other action, puzzle and simulation releases.
facts: The Centre for Computing History preserves eighteen Rainbow Arts game records across Commodore, Atari and Amstrad systems.
Its Commodore 64 collection includes Rock 'n Roll, Volleyball Simulator, The Curse of RA and Turrican II.
note: The museum record demonstrates Rainbow Arts' multi-format publishing activity; developer credits vary between individual releases.

sources.label: Centre for Computing History — Rainbow Arts games

summary: Reaktor was Ariolasoft's action-game imprint and appeared on a small range of mid-1980s 8-bit releases, including Deactivators and Starfox.
facts: The Centre for Computing History describes Deactivators as published through Ariolasoft's action-game imprint Reaktor.
The museum preserves Reaktor-labelled releases on the ZX Spectrum, Commodore 64 and Amstrad CPC, including Starfox and Out of this World.
note: Reaktor is treated as a publishing imprint associated with Ariolasoft rather than as a replacement for the individual development-team credits.

summary: Renegade published a focused range of early-1990s computer games, particularly on the Amiga, working with prominent independent developers including The Bitmap Brothers and Sensible Software.
facts: The Centre for Computing History preserves seven games under the Renegade publishing credit.
Its Amiga collection includes Gods, The Chaos Engine and Sensible World of Soccer releases, with development credited to external teams including The Bitmap Brothers and Sensible Software.
note: Renegade's role was frequently publishing rather than development, so individual developer credits remain separate throughout CCG.

summary: Sega developed from Japan's commercial-amusement industry into one of the major arcade and home-console companies. Its properties also reached Commodore computers through licensed home conversions and publishing arrangements.
facts: Sega's official corporate timeline identifies Nihon Goraku Bussan Co., Ltd., established in June 1960, as the predecessor of today's Sega Corporation.
The company name became Sega Enterprises, Ltd. in 1965 after a merger with Rosen Enterprises, and Sega states that the name derives from 'Service Games'.
The Centre for Computing History preserves Commodore releases carrying Sega properties including Out Run and Tapper.
note: Many Commodore Sega games were converted or distributed by other companies, so CCG retains version-specific developer and regional publisher credits.

sources.label: Centre for Computing History — SEGA Commodore games

summary: Sierra On-Line became a major computer-game publisher associated particularly with graphic adventures. Its catalogue expanded across numerous computer platforms, including Commodore systems.
facts: The Centre for Computing History preserves Sierra On-Line releases across several generations of computer hardware.
Its Commodore Amiga records include Manhunter: New York and Space Quest III, documenting Sierra's presence on the platform during the late 1980s.
note: This profile is deliberately based on institutional catalogue evidence; individual Sierra development teams and designers remain credited at game level.

sources.label: Centre for Computing History — Sierra On-Line Amiga games

summary: Software Projects was a prolific British 8-bit publisher whose catalogue included major home-computer names such as Manic Miner and Jet Set Willy alongside licensed conversions and original games.
facts: The Centre for Computing History preserves thirty-eight game records under the Software Projects publishing credit.
Its Commodore records include Manic Miner, BC's Quest for Tyres, Dinky Doo and Dragon's Lair, demonstrating a catalogue that mixed original software and licensed properties.
note: The CCG archive follows publisher credits for the represented versions rather than assuming one publisher relationship across every platform.

sources.label: Centre for Computing History — Software Projects games

summary: State Soft appears in the CCG archive as a small Commodore 64 publishing label active in the mid-1980s. Surviving reliable company-history material is limited, so the site keeps this profile deliberately modest rather than inventing corporate details.
note: No sufficiently strong first-party or institutional company-history source has yet been located; this entry remains curated archive context rather than a source-backed corporate history.

summary: Storm appears across late-1980s and early-1990s computer publishing credits, with the preserved catalogue covering strategy, action and compilation releases on systems including the Amiga, Atari ST and Amstrad CPC.
facts: The Centre for Computing History preserves Storm-published software including Napoleoni: The Campaigns 1805-1814 on the Commodore Amiga and St Dragon on the Amstrad CPC.
The museum also records Storm in combined publishing credits, reflecting the label's use across different distribution and development arrangements.
note: Several historically distinct Storm-named entities appear in software records, so this profile avoids asserting a single unsupported corporate lineage.

sources.label: Centre for Computing History — Storm games

summary: Strategic Simulations, Inc. (SSI) specialised in computer strategy, wargame and role-playing software. The company's surviving corporate papers are preserved by The Strong museum.
facts: The Strong holds the Joel Billings Strategic Simulations, Inc. papers, a collection of SSI corporate records whose bulk dates run from 1979 to 1996.
The archive identifies SSI with computer games, strategy games, simulations and role-playing material, matching the company's long-running specialisation in those genres.
note: The corporate-history claims here are restricted to information supported by The Strong's SSI archival collection.

sources.label: The Strong — Joel Billings Strategic Simulations, Inc. papers

summary: Synapse Software was an American early-1980s computer-software publisher associated with action games and later interactive-fiction projects, with releases reaching Commodore 64 and Atari systems.
facts: The Centre for Computing History preserves Synapse and Synsoft software including Commodore 64 material and Atari software.
Its collection records Essex under the Synapse publishing credit and Blue Max under Synsoft, illustrating the company's use of different branding in different markets.
note: The archive uses both Synapse and Synsoft credits; CCG retains the publisher name attached to each represented release.
